https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/life.text: Every place, country, city or town has its unique landmark that visitors seek out. For example, Rome in Italy has Trevi Fountain where people toss coins and make a wish. In Prague, they touch historic statues for luck. But in Hungary's capital, Budapest, travellers line up for hours just to rub the belly of a happy-looking bronze statue of a policeman. And they do so because it is believed to bring good luck, prosperity, happiness and safe journeys.Who is this Fat Policeman In Budapest, it is simply known as the Fat Policeman Statue. Itâs a quirky bronze figure which has become one of Budapest's most photographed attractions. Even from far, you can see his shiny rounded belly which shimmers like polished gold. It shines because thousands of hands touch it every year in the hope of receiving a little luck.A travel superstition or not, this smiling policeman statue has become a delightful ritual for visitors exploring Budapest. There are several videos on Instagram, which shows travellers rubbing the fat belly of the statue.Where is the Fat Policeman Statue? The statue stands in the heart of Budapest, at the corner of ZrÃ­nyi Street (ZrÃ­nyi utca) and OktÃ³ber 6 Street (OktÃ³ber 6. utca). For more precise location, itâs just a short walk from St. Stephen's Basilica. The statue can be located easily as visitors can also reach here from the iconic Chain Bridge.The reason behind the belly rub The biggest attraction isn't the statue itself but the tradition surrounding it. As per local belief, rubbing the policeman's belly brings good luck and financial prosperity. It also means safe travels. Some locals also jokingly say it ensures you'll return to Budapest one day, and another legend claims it prevents you from gaining weight. But these are folk beliefs rather than historical facts which have become a prominent part of Budapest travel.Who does the statue represent? Affectionately known as the "Fat Policeman," the bronze sculpture is a life-sized figure depicting a jovial Hungarian policeman. He is wearing a ceremonial uniform inspired by the early 20th century. He also wears a helmet to complete the look. Rather than celebrating law enforcement, the statue captures a humorous side of the city.The present sculpture credits Hungarian sculptor AndrÃ¡s IllyÃ©s and notes the present bronze work was unveiled in 2008.How to reach the statue Nearest landmark: St. Stephen's Basilica (just a one-minute walk)Nearest metro station: Bajcsy-Zsilinszky Ãºt (M1 Metro), around five minutes walkFrom Chain Bridge: Around a 7â10 minute walkFrom the Hungarian Parliament Building: Around 15 minutes on footBecause it sits in Budapest's pedestrian-friendly city centre, most travellers simply discover it while exploring nearby attractions.Best time to visit for photographyFor best photographs and no waiting in line, come as early as possible in the morning or later in the evening. Why travellers love it Visitors love it because they can interact with it. Every person who places a hand on its polished belly becomes part of a tradition and shared experience from around the world. So, if Budapest is on your travel bucket list, don't rush past this smiling bronze officer. Smile for a pic, rub the famous shiny belly for money and luck.Looking for trusted parenting advice? Pimentel / Unsplash Lithuania's State Child Rights Protection and Adoption Service has rejected claims that it decided to remove from a family a two-month-old baby who had already died after suffering from a serious illness. âThe agency said the decision concerned all children in the family because of suspected neglect, and that the parents only received the formal decision after the baby's death because the service was informed of her death several days later. The allegations emerged after the story of a family from UkmergÄ, northeastern Lithuania, spread on social media. People pointed to the perceived absurdity of ordering the removal of a baby girl who had already died, while others accused the authorities of being too heavy-handed in removing all of the family's children or reacting too late. âAccording to the family's account, the two-month-old girl, who had been diagnosed with Patau syndrome, died in hospital in Kaunas. The family said they received the child protection service's decision two days after her death. â Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Lina BaranauskienÄ, head of the Vilnius County Child Rights Protection Division, expressed her condolences to the family and explained why the decision had been made to remove all of the children living in the household. â She said child protection officers were alerted by medical staff after an exhausted two-month-old baby was admitted to hospital. â "Removing a child from their parents is an extreme measure that is taken only in exceptional circumstances, when parents do not cooperate, refuse assistance, no improvement takes place, and the child continues to face a real threat. In this family's case, a decision was made that it was necessary to ensure the children's safety. â "We made the decision on July 27, but only on July 28 did we learn that the baby had died on Sunday, July 26," she said. â BaranauskienÄ added that the service would seek ways to improve communication between hospitals and child protection authorities to prevent similar situations in future. â She stressed that while parents' faith, beliefs and values were their own choice, a child's right to appropriate medical treatment and to life must be protected. â "In this particular case, doctors informed us that the baby had been brought to hospital exhausted and in a critical condition. She required urgent medical attention," she said. â According to BaranauskienÄ, it was not possible to establish a dialogue with the parents, although they were still being invited to cooperate and work with the authorities to find a solution. â She said the decision to remove all the children was based not only on the condition of the baby admitted to hospital, but on the overall circumstances. â "There are additional circumstances which, as I have already mentioned, mean that the children's safety must be ensured. There are concerns about their welfare, emotional security, development and health," she said. â The family had been known to child protection authorities since 2018. The service had previously received several reports, including from medical professionals, concerning inadequate healthcare for the children. â BaranauskienÄ said the family had previously received support from the UkmergÄ Social Services Centre, but had been "difficult to cooperate with" at that time as well. â "If we are still unable to establish any contact with the family in the near future, a decision will be made to remove the children from the family," she said. â She later stressed that the service would not apply to the court to remove the children if an agreement could be reached with the parents. â BaranauskienÄ also noted that home births are legal in Lithuania and confirmed that the baby had been officially registered and had a birth certificate. â The baby's father, Mintautas, told LRT that his daughter had been born with Patau syndrome, a congenital genetic disorder that prevented her from feeding normally. â He said the parents had fed her using a pipette and sought treatment at Kaunas Clinics after noticing that she was not gaining weight. â "Children with Patau syndrome do not usually live long. Most survive only a couple of months, and very few reach adolescence. It is a genetic disorder. An inability to absorb food properly is very common with this syndrome. â "There are also other symptoms, such as a cleft palate, underdeveloped eyes and an underdeveloped atrium of the heart. Many of these were later confirmed by medical tests," he said. â According to Mintautas, the girl spent the first month of her life at home. â "It was important to us that she lived surrounded by love and had the best quality of life possible, that she experienced our touch and everything that family life could offer, for as long as she could. We are grateful that she had a month to experience that. â "The second month was completely different because we could no longer be with our baby. We could only stroke her; we were not allowed to hold her for long periods or breastfeed her in hospital. Those were very painful moments," he said. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/01/lipc.text: Menü Kereső Német belügyminiszter: orosz megbízásból támadhatták meg drónnal a lipcsei repteret Külföld Ághassi Attila Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Oroszország megbízásából kísérelhették meg a támadást a lipcsei repülőtéren a robbanószerrel felszerelt drónnal, de ez szerencsére meghiúsult – közölte Alexander Dobrindt német belügyminiszter a rendőrség vizsgálati eredményeire, elkövetői mintázatokra és hírszerzési értesülésekre hivatkozva kedden Berlinben. Az MTI beszámolója szerint az ügyben Németország újabb Oroszország elleni büntetőintézkedéseket vezetett be, ezt Johann Wadephul német külügyminiszter is megerősítette. Szeptember 18-ig bezáratják a bonni orosz főkonzulátust, valamint a Berlinben működő Orosz Ház kulturális központot, és megszigorítják az orosz állampolgárok beutazására vonatkozó ellenőrzéseket is – jelentette be Wadephul. Bekérették Oroszország berlini nagykövetét is. A német kormány közleménye szerint Oroszország mint a támadás kezdeményezője ellen lépnek fel annak érdekében, hogy megnehezítsék az ilyen jellegű cselekmények további végrehajtását Németországban és az Európai Unióban, ezenfelül szorgalmazzák az EU-nál a további orosz felelősök szankcionálását. A közepes méretű drónon robbanószert is találtak , és az az ukránok hatalmas Antonov teherszállító gépe mellé, a reptér betonjára került. Az erről készült képek, videók az bejárták a világsajtót . Ursula von der Leyen, az Európai Bizottság elnöke találkozik Mark Rutte NATO-főtitkárral, hogy megvitassák az összehangolt válaszlépéseket – erről már az Euronews számolt be. Mark Rutte, a NATO főtitkára azt nyilatkozta, hogy a szervezet teljes mértékben szolidaritást vállal Németországgal. „A bizonyítékok egyértelműek. És üdvözlöm a Németország által válaszul bejelentett intézkedéseket” – írta az X-en. Ursula von der Leyen, az Európai Bizottság elnöke úgy nyilatkozott: „Egységesek vagyunk, kiállunk az orosz agresszió ellen. Elrettentünk mindenkit, aki aláássa szabadságunkat és biztonságunkat.” Az EU is kész arra, hogy további szankciókat készítsen elő Oroszország ellen. Marija Zaharova, az orosz külügyminisztérium szóvivője azt mondta: Moszkva „tükörképszerűen” fog reagálni a német intézkedésekre. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://english.news.cn/20260821/9277f3b.text: Estonia marks 35th anniversary of restoration of independence Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-08-21 04:32:00 TALLINN, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Events were held across Estonia on Thursday to mark the 35th anniversary of the restoration of the country's independence. The main commemorative events took place in the capital with a flag-raising ceremony and the laying of flowers at the Aug. 20 Memorial Stone. The Estonian parliament and the August 20 Club, which brought together surviving members of the Supreme Council who voted for the restoration of independence in 1991, held a joint formal sitting. Estonian President Alar Karis and parliamentary leaders attended the event. In addition, public celebrations were held at the Tallinn TV Tower and the Vabamu Museum of Occupations and Freedom, with family activities, exhibitions and programs recalling the events that led to the restoration of independence. Similar events were also held in cities including Tartu, the second-largest city in Eatonia. On Aug. 20, 1991, the Supreme Council of Estonia adopted a resolution restoring the country's independence from the Soviet Union. ■

Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Firefighters after another massive Russian missile and drone attack against Kyiv on Tuesday. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv books in 1,000 Patriots as UK and EU open up missile aid Germany ‘urgently’ sending PAC-2 interceptors from its stockpile and urges other countries to do the same. What we know on day 1,659 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine is ⁠contracting a supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles over the coming years with the help of allies and ⁠through an E⁠U loan, ​Kyiv’s defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, said on Tuesday as the country’s allies met. Germany announced it is “urgently” sending Ukraine part of its stockpile of Patriot Pac-2 interceptors . Berlin’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, appealed to other supporters of Ukraine “to look into their own stocks and make similar deliveries”. The long-established Pac-2 version destroys ballistic missiles and aircraft by exploding and shredding them with shrapnel, whereas the latest upgrade, the Pac-3, is a higher precision “hit-to-kill” missile that rams into its targets. “I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine,” Pistorius said. “But please, if in doubt, decide in favour for Ukraine .” Before the defence contact group meeting started, the UK announced it had committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences by buying US military equipment that will include Patriot interceptors, write Dan Sabbagh and Jamie Grierson . The commitment also covers large-calibre ammunition and drones. Remilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells Europe Read more Regarding Patriots, Khmara, Kyiv’s defence minister, stressed: “The majority of these [1,000] missiles will only start to be shipped in the coming years, which is why we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today .” The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said Ukraine will ⁠be able to put the ⁠next €3.2bn (£2.7bn; US$3.7bn) disbursement ⁠from the EU’s support ​loan towards ⁠Patriot. Ukraine says it needs 300 Patriot interceptors to defend itself through the winter. Khmara said Ukraine was also being hindered by a shortfall of $27bn in financing for drone supplies. Khmara said Russia was ​making no strategic gains along the 1,200km (750-mile) frontline, but was trying to compensate with “terror against Ukrainians”. Russia resumed its near-constant drone and missile attacks on Kyiv on Tuesday after a brief halt ⁠for the visit of US peace negotiators. Officials said five ​people were killed ​in the capital and more in several regions. There are signs of a successful operation by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps to recapture a Russian-held finger of land near the strategic town of Lyman in the Donetsk region . War analysts said the action liberated more than 200 square kilometres of territory. In a video posted on Monday, Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the corps, stood in the monastery town of Sviatohirsk west of the salient and taunted Putin over the Russian president’s recent claim that Moscow’s forces had captured it. Military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, of the Finland-based Black Bird conflict analysis group, told Reuters that the extent of the Ukrainians’ gains remained unclear. September and October could see the year’s most intense fighting in Donetsk , with Russia potentially trying to stage new mechanised assaults, Michael Kofman of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told Reuters. “As the weather conditions deteriorate, drones become less effective. And that’s usually where Russians try to return mobility to the battlefield.” But Ukraine had developed a solid defence against such attacks, Kofman added, pointing to a failed Russian assault in July near the city of Dobropillia. Russian forces are less than 15km (9 miles) from Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the two main cities in the “fortress belt”. Both are under worsening strikes by drones and guided bombs, regional officials have said. Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump on Tuesday had an hour-long phone call , a summary of which was only available from the Kremlin at time of writing. Trump called for a speedy end to the fighting, said Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov. Putin “pointed out what the Americans could realistically do to bring the hostilities to a swift conclusion” and stressed that Russia had “no aggressive plans” towards Europe. Volodymyr Zelenskyy meanwhile said Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators could meet as early as this month. “If all sides agree, we also want to hold it in the autumn. If September works out, then it would be great. The earlier, the better.” A Bloomberg report predicted no serious moves towards peace by Russia until 2027. Romania’s SRI intelligence service said it prevented a sabotage ⁠operation coordinated by Russia on Romanian territory. “The Russian citizen was instructed by an intermediary to make photo-video materials with targets of ⁠strategic military interest, including Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft ​during their ​presence on the national ​territory.” Suspected Russian agents tried to blow up an Antonov in August at ​Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany. The SRI said: “The ​investigation also ‌revealed that ​the Russian ​Federation continues to use persons from vulnerable categories to carry out such illegal activities.” Russian authorities said they detained a suspect in last week’s shooting of a senior military officer . The Federal Security Service said a 21-year-old Moldovan national was arrested for being allegedly “involved in an assassination attempt” at the behest of Ukrainian intelligence services. Russia’s investigative committee said the officer was shot at least six times on 3 September on the outskirts of Engels. The city in the Saratov region hosts Russian strategic bombers that are used to attack Ukraine.
